title:
Toward Sensory Homeostasis in Autism:
Comparative Evaluation of a Recurrent Signal-to-Memory Hierarchy
content: Background/Objectives: The signal-to-memory (S2M) hierarchy links Ca²⁺-signal construction and decoding to transcriptional and chromatin changes that may modify subsequent neuronal responsiveness and support sensory homeostasis: adaptation to familiar input while preserving sensitivity to meaningful change. We assessed evidence for its involvement in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) pathogenesis and implications for therapeutic target validation. Methods: The prespecified S2M-44 core was compared with 11 monogenic ASD mouse models, an ASD protein-association network, and 106 schizophrenia-prioritized genes. Exact overlap, molecular association, and functional correspondence were distinguished; broader ASD-gene context and four extension candidates were evaluated separately. Results: Four mouse-model genes matched the core, all transcriptional or chromatin regulators. The protein network represented 27 core proteins, including both IP₃ receptors, ITPR1 and ITPR3, recovered as interactors. Separately reported KDM6B and SETD5 studies demonstrated rescue of downstream neuronal defects, with selected behavioral rescue in the SETD5 model. The schizophrenia set shared one core gene and implicated related signaling operations. Conclusions: These findings strengthen the case for pathogenic involvement of connected S2M operations and prioritize IP₃R-mediated Ca²⁺ release for molecular target validation. Demonstrating target-dependent restoration of signaling and adaptive responsiveness across genetically distinct models would establish a mechanistic foundation for drug discovery.
